extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and professionals who want to apply comedy/performance lessons to business or public speaking
extracted.subtask_description: Short-form advice on stand-up comedy performance focused on willingness to fail (bomb), resilience, iteration, and applying those lessons to business or office settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'bomb'
rubrics_metrics.description: In stand up comedy (later extended to performances of all kinds), to "bomb" is when your performance flops in front of an unsupportive audience. Either the joke was bad or the energy from the audience was negative no matter what, or both. A bomb isn't good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes what counts as a failure in performance: a visible flop caused by material or audience energy. Use this to distinguish ordinary misfires from other types of performance issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Willing to Bomb
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians cherish and value their bomb moments; you must be willing to risk bombing in order to begin and to learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post uses a video example (a comic who bombs, then repeats the joke later and eventually gets a huge laugh) to show the value of trying and failing publicly. Treat willingness to fail as a necessary attitude for growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bravery: make the first move
rubrics_metrics.description: The bravery comes at the beginning - making any first move (on stage or in the office) is an act of bravery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiating (trying a joke, speaking first in a meeting) is itself valuable; prioritize taking the first step over fear of immediate success. This is an explicit criterion for evaluating performers/participants: did they initiate?

rubrics_metrics.name: Take failure in stride (resilience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking the failure in stride is the hardest part - accepting that sometimes what you say won't land and moving on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author gives a personal example (throwing out a bomb on purpose to start somewhere). Evaluate performers on their ability to absorb a flop without freezing or quitting, and to treat bombing as process rather than catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push through and iterate until it works
rubrics_metrics.description: Pushing through to make it work is the gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use persistent repetition and refinement (e.g., repeating a joke multiple times, changing delivery) after an initial failure. The Letterman example—trying the joke again until it wins—illustrates iterative persistence as a virtue and metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bombing as a learning accelerator
rubrics_metrics.description: You learn more and you learn faster if you're willing to bomb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate willingness to take risks as linked to the speed and depth of learning. In business contexts, encourage experiments that may 'bomb' so teams gain faster feedback and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply comedy lesson to business: speak up despite fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Lots of times, people don't speak up. They're worried about looking dumb. Comedians don't mind looking dumb. If YOU could learn the same thing... you'll go further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for workplace behavior: preference for risk-averse silence vs. proactive speaking. Assess people on whether they avoid participation to avoid looking foolish or whether they engage despite risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish harmless bombs from harmful speech
rubrics_metrics.description: When I mean 'bomb,' I surely don't mean to say something awful, harmful, etc. None of that. I just mean, 'what if what you say isn't the best idea in the room' kinds of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern warning: risk-taking does not justify offensive or harmful content. Evaluate content for safety/ethics separately from its success/failure as a joke; do not conflate willingness to fail with permission to be abusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional low-stakes 'bombing' to get started
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately throwing out a bomb on purpose because you wanted to start SOMEWHERE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tactical criterion: sometimes it's acceptable to deliberately try material expected to fail to break inertia and gather feedback. Measure whether such intentional failures are used strategically (low-stakes, learning-focused) rather than recklessly.
